title: Acute conjunctivitis
subject: ophthalmology-ent
setting: Primary care, emergency department, eye clinic
summary: Most acute conjunctivitis in adults is viral and self-limiting: no antibiotics. Treat bacterial conjunctivitis with a 5 to 7 day topical antibiotic, allergic with antihistamine or mast-cell stabiliser drops, and gonococcal or chlamydial infection systemically. Visual loss, pain, corneal involvement, contact lens wear or a neonate need same-day ophthalmology.

sections.title: Recognise the type
items: Viral (usually adenovirus): watery discharge, follicles, tender preauricular node, often one eye then the other, recent cold or contact; highly contagious for 10 to 14 days.
Bacterial: mucopurulent discharge with lids stuck together on waking; usually self-limiting in adults. In children examine the ears, as conjunctivitis with otitis suggests Haemophilus influenzae.

Gonococcal: rapid onset of copious purulent discharge with marked lid swelling and chemosis; can perforate the cornea. Chlamydial: follicular conjunctivitis persisting for weeks in a sexually active person.
Allergic: itching is the key symptom; bilateral, watery or stringy discharge, lid swelling, atopy or seasonal pattern.
Herpes simplex: usually unilateral, lid vesicles, follicles, sometimes dendritic corneal staining. Varicella zoster: with chickenpox or ophthalmic zoster.
History to take: onset and laterality, discharge, contact lens wear and hygiene, exposure to an infected person, trauma or chemicals, genital symptoms, atopy, immune status, and drops already used.

sections.title: Red flags: same-day ophthalmology
items: Refer (AAO): visual loss, moderate or severe pain, severe purulent discharge, corneal involvement, conjunctival scarring, no response to treatment, recurrent episodes, history of HSV eye disease, or immunocompromise.

Also refer the same day: photophobia, contact lens wearer with pain, photophobia or reduced vision (possible bacterial or Acanthamoeba keratitis), suspected gonococcal infection, and any neonate (ophthalmia neonatorum requires admission).
Consider mimics that cause pain and reduced vision rather than discharge alone: acute angle-closure glaucoma, keratitis, anterior uveitis, scleritis, chemical injury, foreign body.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Check visual acuity and stain the cornea with fluorescein in every red eye.
Most cases need no laboratory tests. Culture all suspected infectious neonatal conjunctivitis.

Culture and sensitivity for severe, recurrent or chronic purulent conjunctivitis or treatment failure; Gram stain and culture when gonococcus is possible; confirm chlamydia with laboratory testing (NAAT) and test for other sexually transmitted infections.

sections.title: Viral, HSV and allergic conjunctivitis
items: Adenoviral: no antibiotics. Cold compresses, artificial tears and topical antihistamines for comfort; hand hygiene and separate towels.
Topical corticosteroids only under ophthalmology supervision, for severe adenoviral keratoconjunctivitis with membranes or reduced vision; they potentiate HSV and need IOP monitoring.

HSV conjunctivitis: topical ganciclovir 0.15% gel 3 to 5 times daily, or oral aciclovir or valaciclovir; never topical steroids; review within 1 week. Neonatal HSV needs urgent paediatric care (systemic infection is life-threatening).
Allergic: avoid the allergen, cold compresses, lubricants, and a topical antihistamine or dual-action drop (for example olopatadine); mast-cell stabilisers for recurrent or persistent disease.
Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (children with severe itching and giant papillae) may need topical steroids or cyclosporine: refer to ophthalmology.

sections.title: Bacterial conjunctivitis
items: Mild: often resolves without treatment; a 5 to 7 day course of a broad-spectrum topical antibiotic speeds recovery and may allow earlier return to school. No agent is superior; choose the most convenient or least expensive.
Povidone-iodine 1.25% eye drops may be as effective as antibiotic drops where access to antibiotics is limited (AAO).
Moderate to severe (copious pus, pain, marked inflammation): take a swab for Gram stain and culture, and refer; MRSA is increasingly isolated and resists many topical antibiotics.
Contact lens wearers: stop lens wear until the eye is normal; use a fluoroquinolone drop (Pseudomonas cover) and refer at once if there is pain, photophobia, reduced vision or a corneal opacity.
Advise return if there is no improvement in 3 to 4 days.

sections.title: Gonococcal and chlamydial conjunctivitis
items: Gonococcal, adults and adolescents: ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose (CDC 2021; the AAO table quotes 500 mg) plus one saline lavage of the eye; review daily until resolved; add keratitis treatment if the cornea is involved. Treat for chlamydia unless excluded, and treat partners.

Chlamydial, adults: doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days (CDC preferred) or azithromycin 1 g single dose (pregnancy: azithromycin or amoxicillin). Topical therapy alone is inadequate. Treat partners and re-evaluate after treatment.

Neonates: gonococcal ophthalmia, ceftriaxone 25 to 50 mg/kg IV or IM single dose (max 250 mg) and assess for disseminated infection; chlamydial, oral erythromycin or azithromycin (see drugs) and watch for pyloric stenosis.
Gonococcal or chlamydial conjunctivitis in a child beyond the newborn period: consider sexual abuse and involve child protection.

sections.title: Prevention and India
items: Hand washing, no sharing of towels, pillows or eye drops, and cleaning of shared surfaces: adenovirus survives for weeks on surfaces. Limit close contact for 10 to 14 days from onset in the last eye affected.
Neonatal ocular prophylaxis at birth (for example erythromycin 0.5% ointment) prevents gonococcal ophthalmia; screen and treat infected pregnant women.

India: epidemic viral conjunctivitis ('Madras eye', adenoviral or enteroviral acute haemorrhagic conjunctivitis) occurs in large outbreaks; manage supportively and focus on hygiene rather than antibiotic or steroid drops.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Antibiotic drops for viral conjunctivitis.
Steroid or steroid-antibiotic combination drops without slit-lamp examination: they worsen HSV and fungal keratitis and cause glaucoma and cataract. Over-the-counter use is common in India.
Missing microbial keratitis in a contact lens wearer.
Treating a painful unilateral red eye with reduced vision as conjunctivitis.

drugs.name: Chloramphenicol 0.5% eye drops
drugs.dose: 1 drop every 2 hours for the first 48 hours, then every 4 hours while awake, for 5 to 7 days in total
drugs.notes: Bacterial conjunctivitis in adults and children.

drugs.name: Moxifloxacin 0.5% eye drops
drugs.dose: 1 drop three times daily for 7 days
drugs.notes: Contact lens wearers (Pseudomonas cover) or when a fluoroquinolone is preferred.

drugs.name: Olopatadine 0.1% eye drops
drugs.notes: Allergic conjunctivitis (antihistamine with mast-cell stabilising action).

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone
drugs.dose: Adults and adolescents: 1 g IM single dose. Children up to 45 kg: 25 to 50 mg/kg IV or IM single dose (max 250 mg IM). Neonates: 25 to 50 mg/kg IV or IM single dose (max 250 mg)
drugs.notes: Gonococcal conjunctivitis; plus saline lavage. Use cefotaxime 100 mg/kg single dose in neonates receiving IV calcium.

drugs.name: Doxycycline
drugs.dose: 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days
drugs.notes: Chlamydial conjunctivitis in adults. Not in pregnancy or children under 8 years.

drugs.name: Azithromycin
drugs.dose: Adults: 1 g orally single dose. Neonates: 20 mg/kg orally once daily for 3 days
drugs.notes: Chlamydia alternative; preferred option in pregnancy.

drugs.name: Erythromycin (oral)
drugs.dose: 50 mg/kg/day orally in 4 divided doses for 14 days
drugs.notes: Neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis; monitor for infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.

drugs.name: Aciclovir (oral)
drugs.dose: 200 to 400 mg orally five times daily until resolved, with review within 1 week
drugs.notes: HSV conjunctivitis; or valaciclovir 500 mg two or three times daily. Adjust for renal impairment.

drugs.name: Ganciclovir 0.15% eye gel
drugs.notes: HSV conjunctivitis or epithelial keratitis; less toxic to the ocular surface than trifluridine.
